newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-The Who's Entwistle brings art to the road.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-The Who's Entwistle brings art to the road.

text.p: John Entwistle is a man at home on the road. And the road has given him the opportunity to show off 20 years' worth of drawings -- done mostly off the road.

The lanky bass player for The Who told Reuters that after about 20 years of drawing fellow rock stars and other characters he decided to put the prints together and take them on the road with him. "It's easy to do because I'm here," he said.

The show first turned up in the United States this year when Entwistle was touring with his legendary rock band. Since mid-year, his "Who's Art?" shows have been opening simultaneously with the band's performances of its Quadrophenia rock opera in cities such as New York, Denver, San Francisco and Chicago.

The more than 30 pen-and-ink drawings are mainly of other rock stars including fellow Who members Pete Townshend, Roger Daltrey and the late Keith Moon but also include such gems as "the German tourist" and "the American tourist." The exhibit also includes what may be Entwistle's most famous work, the lithograph "Who By Numbers," which was taken from the original drawing featured on the band's 1975 hit album.

The silver-haired bass player said that although the road is his true love, it makes his art suffer. "I can't do any drawing when I'm on tour," he said. "Usually when I get back, if I've got a couple of weeks off, I'll set aside a week of drawing and a week of relaxing. I try and schedule it in big blocks."

The first instalment of a trilogy of novels recounting humorous adventures with The Who has also been long delayed, he said. "I set aside three months to work on the book last year and ended up doing the Ringo Starr tour, and now this one's come along," he said, referring to the band's performance of its 1973 Quadrophenia, the lesser known of its two rock operas.
"The book's third in line behind the artwork and the shows," added Entwistle, who also did that tour with his band in January, February and March of this year.

"It's been an idea of Pete's for quite a long time to do Quadrophenia as a work, to put some more substance into it and perform it in its entirety, which we only did once or twice," he said. "It's nice to be out there playing the whole thing."

The show is really more of an extravaganza, with huge video screens, a five-piece horn section, backup singers and other rock stars such as Billy Idol and Gary Glitter. But for Entwistle, the consummate rock 'n' roller, performing Quadrophenia is a paradox.
"It's good to have a little discipline," he said. "When I'm out with my own band, there's no discipline. It's out and out rock 'n' roll."
But playing with his own band also allows him to take centre stage as often as he likes. And he likes.

"I guess I need the fix of being the boss and playing solos whenever I like," he said, "especially after coming back to this and getting one or two solos in the show. I feel great for like five minutes and then it's back to playing regular bass."
NO SET PLANS AFTER THIS YEAR

The Quadrophenia tour is on a limited engagement but Entwistle said the band is just playing it by ear, so to speak. "We don't have any set plans after this year. I don't know. Something might happen next year."

The Who has been effectively disbanded since the death of drummer Keith Moon in 1978 but did not officially break up until 1982 after putting out a couple of albums with a replacement drummer. In 1989 the band launched a tour Entwistle dubbed the "back from the dead good-bye again tour."

This year he spent two weeks in the studio with his band before rehearsing for the Quadrophenia shows and plans to bring his band back together to work on the album, he said. "If it doesn't look like it's going to get finished by summer, I'll probably stop work on the album and tour again. I want to try and do a summer tour with my band."
As always for Entwistle, the road never stops calling.
